rv.q: It's a fist-pumping joyride – and, just as with the film, we're rooting for them the entire way.

Fortunately, with Neko Case in charge of the music and lyrics, the Young Vic’s production is far removed from the usual musical theatre fare offered up in the West End.

The overall effect is a solid and occasionally charming musical which eschews whimsy in favour of real life jeopardy, and is a female buddy tale which comes close to emulating the shenanigans of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid .
There is a considerable amount of anarchic spirit, but it doesn’t go as far as it could or fully embrace what musical theatre has to offer.
What is meant to be something thrilling and captivating instead ebbs and flows, largely because of musical numbers that add little, if anything at all to the narrative.
But it all feels meagre, slow-paced, stripped of excitement and crucially of that sense of liberation which powers the narrative even as it dips towards its inevitable close.

This adaptation of Thelma and Louise brings this iconic work to a new generation, celebrating a story of freedom and self-discovery that continues to resonate today.
The original storytelling still shines through, but the adaptation struggles to match the power of the story it is telling.
Thelma & Louise is far from a total car crash, but it does make you feel as if it has left you lingering in midair waiting for an impact that never came.

In the end, despite a pair of stellar performances, this tame nostalgia trip sticks to the safety of the middle lane, has an engine that purrs when it should rev, and runs out of gas well before it attains the momentum, heart, and visceral thrill of the source material.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this musical adaptation of the iconic film, with strong lead performances from Tucker and Lennox widely praised but Neko Case's score proving divisive and staging challenges undermining the road movie's cinematic sweep.

vr.q: I do think it's one that fans of new musical theater ought to go and check out.
